subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: Pooja, you asked how I did it. Honestly, I was terrified. It's Ayesha, remember. At the bus-stop shelter an older guy kept crowding a girl who was gripping her bag, and everyone was looking at their phones. I did not shout. I walked up and said, "Hey, there you are!" as if I knew her, and asked her to sit with me. She did, fast. The guy hovered a bit, then wandered off when I stared at the timetable really hard. When the bus came I told the conductor to keep an eye out for her stop. Small stuff. But I keep thinking, I did not have to fight anyone.

qa.q: What did Ayesha say to the girl at the bus stop?
qa.a: Ayesha said, "Hey, there you are!" as if they already knew each other, and asked her to sit down.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling when walking up to the girl?
qa.a: Ayesha was terrified but chose a low-risk action; the words "honestly, I was terrified" show the fear was real even though the action was small.

qa.q: Why did Ayesha's approach work without a confrontation?
qa.a: Ayesha gave the girl a way out and a companion, and asked the conductor to look out for her stop, small safe steps rather than an all-or-nothing act of heroism.

qa.q: What might the girl have felt when Ayesha said "Hey, there you are!" and offered a seat?
qa.a: The girl probably felt relief and safety; sitting fast suggests she was glad someone had noticed and given her an easy way to leave the situation.

grounding: A teenager chooses a low-risk action such as checking on the target and distracting the aggressor, showing safe helping is a range of options.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: I was on the metro platform watching everything, and here is what I saw. A man had grabbed a boy's phone out of a group of schoolkids and was jeering at them. Six or seven commuters stood around. Jahnavi, a girl in a college lanyard, did not shout. She walked up to the boy, asked, "Are you okay? Do you want to call someone?" and stood next to him. Deepika, another passenger, quietly pressed the help button at the pillar and spoke to the station staff. The man saw the two of them and the staff coming and dropped the phone. Jahnavi stayed beside the boy until the guard arrived.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi ask the boy?
qa.a: Jahnavi asked, "Are you okay? Do you want to call someone?"

qa.q: Why might Jahnavi have chosen to stand next to the boy instead of shouting?
qa.a: Jahnavi seems to want to help calmly and safely, showing care for the boy first; standing beside him signals support without provoking the man.

qa.q: What small action by Deepika made a difference?
qa.a: Deepika pressed the help button and told the station staff, a low-risk action that brought adults in without any confrontation.

qa.q: What might the boy have been feeling before and after Jahnavi stood beside him?
qa.a: The boy was probably scared and embarrassed before, and relieved afterwards that someone checked on him and stayed until the guard arrived.

grounding: A teenager and another passenger choose low-risk actions, checking on the target and calling for help, seen by a bystander.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage:
Monday: In the canteen, Aakash's gang snatched Yash's chips and poured them on his head. Thomas felt his fists clench, but fighting would make it worse. After the gang left, he sat beside Yash. “You okay? Want some of mine?” Yash nodded, barely.
Wednesday: Aakash started again. Thomas called out, casually, “Aakash! Coach is looking for you about the team list.” Aakash left, frowning. Yash let out a breath.
Friday: It was worse, and Aakash shoved Yash. Thomas went straight to Mr Varghese on canteen duty. “Sir, Yash needs help near the water cooler.” Mr Varghese went over at once, separated them and took Aakash to the vice-principal. He called Yash's parents that afternoon.

qa.q: What did Aakash's gang pour on Yash's head?
qa.a: They poured Yash's chips on his head.

qa.q: How did Yash seem to feel when Thomas sat beside him?
qa.a: He seemed shaken and quiet, nodding barely, but probably a little comforted to have someone check on him.

qa.q: Which of Thomas's actions were safe, and why?
qa.a: Checking on Yash, distracting Aakash with a message, and getting a teacher were all low-risk choices that helped without starting a fight.

qa.q: How might Aakash see Thomas's call about the coach?
qa.a: Aakash probably didn't realise it was a distraction and just felt annoyed at being interrupted.

grounding: Shows a teenager choosing low-risk ways to help a bullied classmate: checking on him, distracting the bully and calling an adult.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage:
Pranav, sit, I want to tell you something from my school days. I'm your Jagdish mama, and at your age I was no hero.
There was a boy in our class, Ravi, whom the seniors used to trouble every day after PT. I couldn't fight them. They were twice my size.
One day I just walked over after they left and sat with Ravi on the steps. Said nothing much. The next day, when they started, I shouted, “Ravi, PT sir is calling you!” They let him go.
The third time, I went to PT sir himself. He spoke to the seniors that same day and made Ravi a class monitor, which gave him some standing.
Small things, Pranav. None of them brave. All of them useful.

qa.q: What did young Jagdish shout on the second day?
qa.a: He shouted, "Ravi, PT sir is calling you!"

qa.q: How did young Jagdish feel about fighting the seniors?
qa.a: He felt afraid and powerless, since they were twice his size and he knew he couldn't fight them.

qa.q: What turning point in the story brought lasting help?
qa.a: Going to PT sir himself, who spoke to the seniors that day and made Ravi a monitor.

qa.q: How might Ravi have felt when Jagdish sat with him on the steps?
qa.a: He probably felt less alone and grateful that someone cared, even without many words.

grounding: An elder recalls helping a bullied classmate through small safe steps: sitting with him, distracting the bullies and calling a teacher.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage:
Rain lashed the bus stop outside the school, and the last bus was late. Forty students crammed under the tin roof. Two older boys had Pankaj pinned against the pole, flicking water at him and snatching his umbrella.
Jomon's heart thumped. He couldn't push through the crowd, and fighting would be stupid. He did the easiest thing first. “Pankaj! Your mother's on the phone for you!” he shouted, holding up his own phone.
The boys hesitated. Pankaj slipped free and squeezed next to Jomon.
Then Jomon called the school security desk. “There's trouble at the bus stop, can someone come?” The guard came with an umbrella in three minutes and stood with them till the bus arrived.

qa.q: How many students were under the tin roof?
qa.a: Forty students crammed under the tin roof.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling as he watched?
qa.a: His heart thumped, so he felt nervous and tense, but he was determined to help safely.

qa.q: Why was Jomon's pretend phone call a smart choice?
qa.a: It interrupted the boys without a fight and gave Pankaj a chance to slip free, and calling security then brought an adult.

qa.q: How might Pankaj have felt standing next to Jomon?
qa.a: He likely felt relieved and safer, with someone beside him until the guard came.

grounding: Shows a teenager in a crowded, rainy bus stop using small safe steps: a distraction and a call to security.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage:
The bus stop outside the colony gate was packed at six. Sonali noticed a man in a grey jacket leaning too close to a girl in school uniform, murmuring. It was Jyoti from the tuition batch below hers, edging away and clutching her file. People around them scrolled their phones.
Sonali's first thought was to shout at him. Her second was that he was much bigger than her. She chose something smaller.
She walked up and said brightly, "Jyoti! There you are, Ma'am's waiting for us," stepped between them and took Jyoti's elbow. The man turned away.
Round the corner, Sonali asked, "Are you okay?" Jyoti nodded, eyes wet. Sonali waved over the traffic warden at the signal and pointed out the grey jacket, then called Jyoti's mother and stayed with her until she arrived.

qa.q: What did Sonali say to get Jyoti away from the man?
qa.a: "Jyoti! There you are, Ma'am's waiting for us."

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling before she stepped in?
qa.a: Sonali felt angry enough to want to shout, but also scared because the man was much bigger, so she chose a safer move.

qa.q: Why was Sonali's small action wiser than shouting at the man?
qa.a: It got Jyoti out quickly without a confrontation, and then brought in the warden and Jyoti's mother.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Jyoti when Sonali appeared?
qa.a: Jyoti was probably frightened and relieved at once, glad not to be alone in a crowd that was looking at phones 🤍

grounding: Shows a teenager choosing low-risk ways to help, distracting the harasser, checking on the target and calling adults, rather than an all-or-nothing rescue.
